sections.report:
**Walk: The whole piece** (one screen, about 1280×800, so no crops needed)

- Can a first-time viewer say in one sentence what it is for: yes. It is service notes for people taking the river ferry.
- Do the main image and headline make one idea: yes. There is no image, so the line does not apply.
- Does every element do a job: yes. There is a heading and three paragraphs, with no rules, boxes or ornament.
- Do type, colour and shape share one mood: yes. One sans serif in near-black on white.
- Is the copy finished: yes. I found no placeholder text and no spelling mistakes.
- Do repeated elements look the same: yes. All three paragraphs are set the same way.
- Does the mood fit the message: yes. Plain and calm suits practical notice text.
- Does each heading name what its section holds: yes. "Notes for ferry passengers" matches the content.

No line is `no` or `unsure`, so there are no entries to open.

**Section.** The whole piece: applies.

**Findings**
None.

Below the checklist, a copy point for the director: the times a passenger acts on are vague. "Between early morning and late evening" (y≈190), "every forty minutes" with no starting time (y≈145–190), and "the last crossing leaves the quay before dusk" (y≈502) do not let a reader work out when the first or last boat goes. "Before dusk" moves through the winter and could mean any time in the hour before it. A reader who guesses wrong misses the last boat. "The market quay" also leaves it unclear whether the last winter crossing runs in one direction or both.

This is a defect, judged as common sense with no catalog entry. Weight: major, because timetable facts are what this notice is for. Fix direction: give clock times for the first and last crossings (summer and winter), name which landing the last boat leaves from, and anchor the 40-minute cycle to a departure time such as ":00, :40, :20".

**What's working.**
- It reads as one plain thing. There is one typeface, one text colour and one heading over three paragraphs, with no decoration, so nothing distracts from the notes.
- The heading "Notes for ferry passengers" says who it is for and what it holds, so a reader knows straight away whether it concerns them.

**Checklist.** The whole piece: 8 lines, 8 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure

sections.report:
Walk (working notes):
First read: the eye lands on the bold title "Notes for ferry passengers" (top left, about y 58–97), then drops into three short paragraphs of body text. It reads as a short information page for ferry users. It feels calm and plain. Assumed job: give passengers practical facts about the timetable, bicycles and winter service.

What matters first:
- One element dominates? Yes. The title is bold, about 36 px against body text of about 19 px, and darker.
- Levels distinct, no near-same sizes? Yes. There are only two levels, title and body, with a big step between them.
- Headings differ in more than size? Yes. The title is also heavier and slightly darker.

No line was answered no or unsure, so I skipped step 5.

---

**Section.** What matters first: applies.

**Findings**
None.

**What's working.**
1. **The title is clearly the starting point.** "Notes for ferry passengers" (x 120–567, y 58–97) is about twice the body size and much heavier, so the eye knows where to start. Nothing else on the page competes with it.
2. **The type scale is just two clearly different levels.** The title and the body are far apart in size, weight and darkness, so neither looks like a mistake. That suits three short paragraphs. Note for the director: the three paragraphs cover separate topics (timetable, bicycles, winter). If the page grows, short subheads would help readers scan, but at this length nothing is lost. Also, the very loose line spacing (lines about 45 px apart, paragraph gaps about 64 px) makes the paragraphs hard to tell apart as groups. That belongs to arrangement and text, not to this section.

**Checklist.** What matters first: 3 lines, 3 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure

**Section.** Arrangement and space: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Is the space inside each group clearly smaller than the space between groups, so each heading sits nearer the text it introduces?** No. In the body column (x≈120–750, y≈130–515), lines within a paragraph sit about 45 px apart (baselines at about 145, 190 and 236), and paragraphs sit about 64 px apart (236→300, 391→456). The step between paragraphs is only about 1.4× the line pitch. On top of that, the line spacing is very loose, so each line already floats on its own. The result is that the viewer sees eight evenly spaced lines rather than three paragraphs, and has to read to find where one note ends and the next begins. On a page of separate notes (timetable, bicycles, winter), that separation is the structure. Equal gaps erase groups (Wertheimer's proximity rule, via Arnheim, *Art and Visual Perception*, ch. II). Fix: tighten the line spacing within paragraphs to a normal reading spacing, and keep the paragraph gap clearly larger, about a full blank line or more, so each note reads as one block. **Defect. Weight: major.** The even, loose spacing is the main thing that makes the page look like a stack of lines rather than three notes.
2. **Does the visual weight balance, with no side, crowded or empty, that makes the page look about to tip?** No. All the content sits in the upper-left area (x 120–750, y 55–515). The right side (x≈760–1280) and the bottom (y≈520–800) are empty, and nothing on the light side counters the heavy one. In this frame the page looks unfinished or slid to one side more than deliberately asymmetric. A heavy side needs a counterweight (Arnheim, *Art and Visual Perception*, ch. I "Balance"). A left-aligned reading column on a wide screen is common on the web, so this costs little if the page really sits in a wider site layout. Fix: either center the column in the viewport or give the right side a job, such as a small timetable box or the landing names, so the asymmetry looks chosen. **Convention, leaning taste. Weight: minor.**

**What's working.**
- Everything shares one left edge at x≈120, the heading and all three paragraphs. That gives the page a clean, unbroken reading line, so keep it in any revision.
- The column is about 630 px wide, a comfortable reading measure. The arrangement leads the eye straight down with nothing pulling it away.

**Checklist.** Arrangement and space: 13 lines, 11 yes, 2 no (space inside groups smaller than between groups; visual weight balances)

The Text section review is done. There is one finding, and the full report follows.

**Section.** Text: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Does the space between lines of a paragraph suit its line length, neither cramped nor so loose that the lines drift apart?** No. In all three paragraphs (x 120–750), lines are about 45 px apart (baselines near y 145, 190, 236; 300, 346, 391; 456, 502) on body text that looks about 18–19 px. That is roughly 2.4× the type size. At a moderate line length of about 60–70 characters, this is about double what the measure needs. The viewer sees each line as a separate strip rather than a paragraph, and has to hunt for the start of the next line. There is a second cost. The space between paragraphs is about 64 px from one baseline to the next, only about 19 px more than the space between lines. So the paragraph breaks barely register, and the page reads as eight evenly spaced lines rather than three grouped notes. Source: Bringhurst, *The Elements of Typographic Style* §2.2.1, and Hochuli, *Detail in Typography*, p. 47: line spacing should match the measure, and this measure doesn't need this much. Fix: bring line spacing down to about 1.4–1.6× the type size, and keep a clearly larger gap between paragraphs, roughly one blank line, so each note reads as one block. Type: convention. Weight: major. It is the one thing that makes this otherwise clean page read worse than it should.

**What's working.**
- **Line length:** lines run about 60–70 characters, within Bringhurst's 45–75 range, so the column is comfortable once the spacing is fixed.
- **Type plan:** one plain sans family is used throughout. A bold heading over regular dark text gives a clear two-level scale with strong contrast, and nothing competes.

**Checklist.** Text: 30 lines, 29 yes, 1 no (space between lines of a paragraph).

**Walk (working notes).** First read: the eye lands on the bold heading "Notes for ferry passengers", then moves down three short paragraphs of grey-black sans text in a left column on plain white. It reads as a simple informational note for ferry riders. It feels calm and plain. Job (assumed): a short web notice telling passengers about the timetable and bicycle rules. Bash was refused, so I worked from the whole image (about 1280×800, one screen).

Color:
- Small palette: yes. One neutral range only: white ground, near-black heading, dark grey body text.
- Saturated color kept small: yes. There is no saturated color.
- Clear light/dark range: yes. Dark text on white keeps full structure in grayscale.
- Warm forward / cool recede: yes. Not applicable, since there are no hues.
- Matching colors look the same: yes. The body text looks the same grey in all three paragraphs.
- No vibrating edges: yes.
- Status colors used for their usual meaning: yes. There are none.
- Color meaning also shown another way: yes. No meaning is carried by color.
- Dark theme uses gray, not black: yes. Not a dark theme.

No line came out `no` or `unsure`, so no entries need opening.

---

**Section.** Color: applies, but only barely. The piece is entirely neutral: dark text on a white ground, with no hues.

**Findings**
None.

**What's working.** The palette is only white and two dark neutrals. The heading (about x 120–568, y 58–96) is the darkest, heaviest element. The body text is a slightly softer near-black that still looks high-contrast on white. With no hue competing, everything is ranked by value and weight alone, so the page reads the same in grayscale and gets in the way of nothing.

**Checklist.** `Color: 9 lines, 9 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure`
